transport.shape: flat: every field sits alongside `type`, no envelope
transport.firstServerFrame: serverInfo, ahead of every reply; unsolicited activity broadcasts for sessions that already existed may precede it

capabilities.notes: A gate entry is a message `type`, or `type.field` for a capability that gates one optional field of an otherwise ungated message. The field form exists because an old core still runs a frame whose field it does not know, so a client has to be able to ask beforehand whether the field will be honoured. The gate is also what says WHICH core speaks a message: see the CATALOGUE_IS_THE_UNION rule.

create.notes: cols/rows omitted means the core picks its own spawn grid. `model` pins the CLI to one model for this spawn (the desktop's model setting, and the `model` an Oracle dispatch line asks for); it is gated by `spawnModel`, and omitting it, sending null, or sending an empty string all mean the CLI's own default, which is also what a core without the capability does with it. `initialInput` is a prompt to deliver, not bytes to write: the core pastes it and sends the submitting Enter itself, once it has confirmed the paste landed, so a client never appends a newline of its own. A core that only writes the text leaves the agent with the prompt typed and unsent, and nothing runs. `preset` names a per-spawn instruction set and is gated by `spawnPreset`. It is a NAME, never prose: the three CLIs expose nothing in common here, so one name means three mechanisms - claude takes `--append-system-prompt` with the body the core reads from its preset directory, codex takes `--profile <name>` layering a config the user owns, opencode takes `--agent <name>` naming an agent the user defined. Only claude's is an APPEND; the other two select something the user wrote, which is what keeps this inside the prime directive - the core never authors a CLI's config. A name the core cannot resolve is an error, not a silent drop: a preset the client asked for and the core swallowed is the same class of bug `spawn-model` exists to catch. Replies created + attached, or error.

reactivate.notes: The resume path: answers `attached` when the prior CLI conversation came back, and `unresumable` when there is no conversation id to resume. A core MAY self-heal a pinned id whose transcript never got written by booting fresh instead (the Swift core does), so a client that specifically WANTS a fresh conversation must ask for one with `restartFresh` rather than infer it here.

restartFresh.notes: Restart an exited session as a brand-new CLI conversation under the same juancode id, discarding the prior one, and answer `attached` for it. Unlike `reactivate` it needs no resumable conversation id, so it has no `unresumable` leg, and it carries no prior scrollback: the conversation the session is leaving behind is the point. A core that pins its own session ids pins a NEW one, so the restarted session is resumable from its first completed turn. Only defined for a session that is not running: on a live one the core answers `error` rather than throwing the running conversation away. See ADDITIVE_FIELDS for why this is a message and not a flag on reactivate.

input.notes: seq present means the core must reply with a matching inputAck; absent means no ack.

resize.notes: seq present means the core must reply with a matching resizeAck.

editQueued.notes: Replace a still-pending message's text in place, addressed by the id its last `queue` snapshot gave it. Not a cancel-and-requeue: the occurrence keeps its id, its position in delivery order and the surface it arrived from, so editing the third message in a queue does not send it to the back of one nobody asked to reorder. Answered with the whole new `queue` snapshot, or with an `error` whose message is `queue-item-not-found` (no pending occurrence has that id, which includes one already claimed for delivery) or `queue-item-not-text` (the occurrence holds key bytes rather than text). Gated separately from `queue` because it is a separate promise: `queue` says messages can be queued and will be typed, `queueEdit` says every occurrence has an id that survives being rewritten, and a core with the first and not the second is not a liar.

subscribeTranscript.notes: Watch a session's structured transcript: the history the core kept, answered at once as one `transcript` frame with `replay: true`, and every record read afterwards as live batches until `unsubscribeTranscript` or the socket closes. Per connection, like `subscribeQueue` and `subscribeScreen`; a second subscribe on the same connection is not a second baseline. A session with no transcript is answered with an empty replay rather than silence, so a client draws an empty panel instead of waiting for a frame that is not coming. This is a SECOND data plane beside the pty bytes: `attached.scrollback` is unchanged and stays what a pane repaints from.

setReaperPolicy.notes: The Settings idle window and the live-session ceiling for a core that reaps in its own process. Every field is optional and only the ones present are applied, so a client with just an idle-window stepper does not have to invent a ceiling. windowMs is the precise spelling of the same quantity as minutes and wins when both are sent; it exists because a core in a separate process can only be told exactly through a frame. 0 in either spelling disables idle reaping, and the ceiling is separate and keeps applying. There is no reply: the effect is visible as sessionMeta frames carrying dormant, and as the exit that follows one.

setReaperProtectedIds.notes: The sessions this client says must never be slept: the pane it has open and the active Oracle. Replaces this connection's whole set - never a patch - and an empty list clears it. Scoped to the connection, so a client that goes away stops protecting a pane nobody is looking at; a core that kept it would make those sessions permanently un-reapable.

serverInfo.notes: Frame 0 on every connection. Nothing precedes it, not even the unsolicited activity broadcasts for sessions that were already live, so a client always knows the version and capability list before it has to interpret anything. See the SERVER_INFO_ORDERING rule. clientId is this connection's grid-ownership token, present on a core that advertises gridOwner: it is the value that comes back as the owner of gridChange and resizeAck when this connection holds the grid, and without it a client can see who drives the grid but not whether that is itself. daemon is who the core process is - { pid, startedAt, exePath, buildStamp, version, buildId, dataDir, sessionsPerProject, ownerState, ownerPid, ownerGraceMs } - and is present only on a core that runs as a separate process from its client, because that is the only kind that can be stale relative to it. The three owner fields are the lifetime half of that: ownerState is owned | orphaned | unowned, ownerPid is the process that will reap it, and ownerGraceMs is how long the core waits after that process is gone before ending itself (0 disables it). They are live rather than captured at boot, because ownership changes hands when a later launch claims a running core, and a core reporting unowned is the one that can outlive every client and go stale. A client compares it against its own launch time, build stamp and environment and says so when they disagree; an in-process core omits the key entirely. Every value inside may be null, which means unknown and never means agreement.

attached.notes: Also re-sent as a repaint when a stalled connection's output buffer overflowed.

screen.notes: reset: true carries every row; reset: false only the changed rows. Geometry or alt-buffer flips force a reset.

resizeAck.notes: applied: the grid reached a live pty. denied: another client owns the shared grid, so re-sending is futile. owner (gridOwner cores): who holds the grid after the arbitration, so a denied client learns who to wait for; string | null, always present as a key, null for an unclaimed grid and for the unarbitrated ephemeral editor/terminal ptys.

gridChange.notes: Broadcast to every connection whenever the arbitrated grid changes hands: a resize granted, or an owner letting go (its pane torn down, its connection closed). owner is string | null and is always present as a key; null means the grid is unclaimed again. Also sent once per already-owned session when a connection opens, so a client arriving mid-flight starts from the truth rather than assuming the grid is free. NOT sent for an unclaimed grid on connect: silence already means nobody is driving. resizeAck is the private answer to one client's request; this is the shared state.

exit.notes: exitCode is number | null and is always present as a key.

activity.notes: state is busy | idle | waiting_input. changes rides only the settle edge; both optionals are omitted, not null.

sessionMeta.notes: A session's persisted meta changed out of band: a title landing from the CLI-title poll or an OSC 0/2 window title, a rename, an archive or dormant flip. Carries the whole SessionMeta — replace the row wholesale, do not patch fields. created and attached remain the snapshot; this is the delta, so a client's session row is not frozen at whatever meta it attached with. Editor sessions are included, unlike activity: a meta edit is not a turn.

transcript.notes: Structured transcript records for one session, oldest first. Two kinds of frame, one shape: `replay: true` is the history a `subscribeTranscript` is answered with, `replay: false` is a batch the core has just read. A record carries at least `session`, `source`, `seq` and `kind`, plus the fields of its kind; the eight kinds are turnStart, turnEnd, step, assistant, thinking, toolCall, toolResult and usage. Append by `seq`, never replace: `seq` is append-only per session and never repeats, restarts included, so a client's whole job is to drop a `seq` it already holds. That is also why a record may legitimately arrive twice, once in a replay and again live when a subscribe lands mid-poll, and why it costs a client nothing.

trackedPrs.notes: The whole watch list, replaced wholesale. Sent once in answer to subscribeTrackedPrs and after that only when the list changed. See TRACKED_PRS_ARE_CHANGES.

rules: An unrecognised client `type` is ignored, never fatal: a newer client must not be able to kill the connection.
Malformed JSON gets one error frame and the connection stays open.
A client feature-detects off serverInfo.capabilities and must refuse a core whose protocolVersion it does not implement.

SERVER_INFO_ORDERING: serverInfo is frame 0. Nothing may precede it: not a reply frame (created, attached, output, screen, inputAck, resizeAck, exit, queue, editorReady, terminalReady, unresumable, error, trackedPrs), and not an unsolicited activity broadcast either. A core must queue the handshake before it starts the activity fan-out, so a connection opened while other sessions are already live still reads serverInfo first and their activity after it.

TRACKED_PRS_ARE_CHANGES: a trackedPrs frame is the whole watch list, replaced wholesale, and it is a change notification. A core sends one snapshot in answer to subscribeTrackedPrs, and after that only when the list it would send differs from the one that connection was last sent. A poll pass that found nothing, or any other internal refresh that moved nothing, sends no frame at all: an identical list carries no information, and a redundant one races whatever the client asks for next, so a client that untracks a PR is answered by a snapshot that still lists it as watched.
A cursor-only change (show/hide, a move with no cell damage) is not guaranteed its own screen frame; it rides the next frame that carries damage.

A new server frame is additive within a protocol version: a client ignores a `type` it does not know, exactly as a core ignores an unknown client `type`. So gridChange and sessionMeta arrived in v1 without a version bump, gated by capability strings a client feature-detects rather than by a new version. A version bump is for a change that alters or removes what an existing frame already means.

ADDITIVE_FIELDS: a new OPTIONAL FIELD on an existing frame is additive within a version too, but it fails differently from a new frame type. A core that does not implement the field still runs the frame without it and answers exactly as it would have, so the field may only be added when ignoring it leaves a defensible default (create.model falls back to the CLI's own model), and it carries a capability string so a client can tell "this core honours it" from "this core will drop it". An operation whose ignored form would be a DIFFERENT operation gets a frame type of its own instead, because an unknown type is ignored whole and the client can see the silence: that is why restarting a session as a fresh conversation is `restartFresh` and not a `fresh` flag on `reactivate`, which an old core would answer by resuming the conversation the client asked to discard.

CATALOGUE_IS_THE_UNION: this file catalogues the PROTOCOL, which is the union of what the cores speak, not the surface of any one of them. A message only one core implements is listed here like any other, and its capability gate is what says which: `drift.test.ts` reads each core's own source, works out the messages its advertised capability list entails, and requires that core to implement exactly those and nothing off this catalogue. So a core that advertises a capability must answer every frame the gate names (no empty promises), and a frame either core speaks must be described here (no drift) - but a core is never asked to grow a decode case, or an encoder it would never use, for a capability it does not advertise. The rule this replaced made the catalogue a mirror of WireProtocol.swift, which left `editQueued` and the transcript frames implemented, advertised and unlistable, and therefore unmeasurable: a golden transcript may only reference catalogued types, so the only planes with no scenario were the ones only one core had.

decisions.process-group reap: No frame, and the `orphan-reap` scenario asserts it off the wire instead. Whether a kill reached the helpers the agent spawned is a fact about a process tree, and `childPid` below already settles that a pid does not cross the wire — so there is nothing a client could be told here that it could act on. The `exit` frame is the closest thing, and it deliberately reports the CHILD's status: a core that killed only the child would still send an identical exit, which is exactly the bug the scenario exists to catch, so widening `exit` would hide it rather than express it. The assertion instead reads the pid the fake agent records, the same side channel `TRANSCRIPT` uses in the other direction. Both cores answer it today with `killpg` escalating to SIGKILL (`PtyProcess.terminate`, `pty.rs::signal_group`); the scenario is what stops the Rust port of JuancodeServices from quietly dropping it.
decisions.childPid: Deliberately never on the wire. A pid from another process is not addressable, and from another machine it is meaningless. The one caller (the desktop's agent-worktree detection, which matches `git worktree list` output against the pty child's pid) degrades to no detection when a core answers nil, and falls back to the session cwd. If that detection has to work against a remote core, the operation moves core-side — the core knows both the pid and the cwd — and the answer surfaces as a SessionMeta field, so still no pid crosses the wire.
decisions.submit / insert: Core-side, not composed by the client. They are not `input` plus a delay: the core delivers a bracketed paste and verifies it landed against the session's headless VT model, retrying on the checks in between, and reports a PasteOutcome. A client reimplementing that needs the model, the retry timing and the failure taxonomy. The remote path is a client frame asking the core to run it, plus an outcome frame; neither exists yet.
decisions.autoSubmit: Core-side, same reasoning as submit, more strongly: it retries across the CLI's boot window until the input box exists. Today it is reachable over the wire only at create time, via create.initialInput, which cannot serve a session that already exists.
decisions.kickQueue: Core-side. The pending-message queue lives in the core and flushes on the idle edge; there is nothing for a client to compose. It needs a client frame of its own (the `queue` capability's fourth verb), which does not exist yet.
decisions.setTitle / setArchived / releaseGrid: Core-side operations with no client frame yet. A remote client can observe all three landing (sessionMeta, gridChange) but cannot cause them: a rename and an archive flip have no wire message and no REST route, and a grid release only happens when the owning connection closes. Filed rather than guessed at here.
decisions.restartFresh grid: restartFresh takes cols/rows like attach and reactivate rather than reusing the grid the session died at: the client that asks for the restart is the one about to render it, and the CLI wraps its first turn at the spawn width forever.
decisions.contributions: The Rust core decodes `subscribeContributions`, `unsubscribeContributions` and `activateContribution` and encodes `contributions` and `contributionResult`, and they are deliberately absent from this catalogue, because it withholds the `contributions` capability: nothing renders a descriptor yet, and advertising it would promise chrome nothing draws. Under CATALOGUE_IS_THE_UNION an unadvertised frame is not on the wire as far as any feature-detecting client is concerned, so it is not catalogued either - which is why `drift.test.ts` carries the five type names in one explicit list with this reason attached. The day the capability is advertised, that list is what makes the suite go red until this file describes them.
decisions.sleepAndWake: Sleeping a session has no frame of its own, and waking it has no frame beyond reactivate. A reap is not a command a client sends; it is something the core decides, and what a client needs to see is the outcome - a sessionMeta carrying dormant: true, followed by the session's exit. Waking is reactivate, which already answers with the woken row. A dedicated sleep/wake pair would be a second way to say what kill and reactivate already say, and a second way for the two to disagree.
